model: A computer program that learned patterns from examples, instead of being given fixed rules.
training: Showing a model many pictures with the right answers, so it adjusts itself until it gives right answers by itself.
dataset: A folder of pictures together with the correct answer (label) for every picture.
label: The correct answer written down for one picture. For us: a box around an object plus its class name.
annotation: The work of drawing the label boxes by hand. Same thing as labelling.
class: One kind of thing a model can name, such as 'motorcycle' or 'license_plate'.
bounding box: A rectangle drawn around an object: where it starts (x, y) and how wide and tall it is.
object detection: Finding every object of known kinds in a picture and drawing a box around each one.
YOLO: 'You Only Look Once'. A fast family of object detectors that find all objects in a single pass over the picture.
YOLOv8n: The smallest ('nano') model of YOLOv8: about 3 million adjustable numbers, fast enough for a normal laptop.
Ultralytics: The company and Python library that provides YOLOv8 and the tools to train and export it.
COCO: A famous public photo collection with 80 everyday object kinds (person, car, bus, truck...). Many models start from it.
pretrained: A model that already learned general seeing skills from a huge dataset before we use it.
fine-tuning: Training a pretrained model a little more on our own pictures so it learns our task.
transfer learning: Re-using what a model learned on one task (everyday objects) to learn a new task (helmets) with much less data.
epoch: One full pass through all the training pictures.
batch: The number of pictures the model looks at together before it adjusts itself once.
image size: The square size in pixels (for example 640 x 640) that pictures are resized to before the model sees them.
learning rate: How big each adjustment step is. Too big and the model overshoots, too small and it learns slowly.
optimizer: The method that decides how the model's numbers are changed after each batch.
early stopping: Stopping training when the score has not improved for a set number of epochs (called patience).
augmentation: Making extra training pictures by changing existing ones (flip, brighten, rotate, zoom) so the model copes with variety.
mosaic: An augmentation that pastes four pictures into one, so the model sees objects in new surroundings.
split: Dividing the pictures into train (to learn from), validation (to check while training) and test (kept sealed for the final honest score).
validation set: Pictures the model does not train on. They are used during training to pick the best moment to stop.
test set: Pictures that are never used for training or choosing. They give the final, honest score.
overfitting: When a model memorises its training pictures and then does badly on new ones.
data leakage: When the same (or almost the same) picture sits in both training and testing. The score then looks better than it really is.
near-duplicate: A picture that is almost identical to another one, such as the next frame of a video or a resized copy.
perceptual hash: A short fingerprint of how a picture looks. Pictures that look alike get fingerprints that are close.
quarantine: Moving a suspect file to a side folder instead of deleting it, so nothing is ever lost.
precision: Of everything the model reported, the share that was correct. High precision means few false alarms.
recall: Of everything that was really there, the share the model found. High recall means few misses.
IoU: Intersection over Union: how much two boxes overlap, from 0 (not at all) to 1 (exactly the same box).
mAP: Mean Average Precision: one number from 0 to 1 for how well a detector finds and boxes objects, averaged over all classes.
mAP@50: mAP where a box counts as correct if it overlaps the true box by at least 50% (IoU 0.5). The score our thesis targets.
mAP@50-95: A stricter mAP that averages the score over overlaps from 50% to 95%. It rewards tight, accurate boxes.
confidence: The model's own certainty for one detection, from 0 to 1.
NMS: Non-Maximum Suppression: when several boxes cover the same object, keep the most confident one and drop the rest.
letterbox: Resizing a picture without changing its shape: the rest of the square is filled with grey, so nothing is stretched.
fitness: The score Ultralytics uses to choose the best saved epoch: 10% of mAP@50 plus 90% of mAP@50-95.
F1: A single score that balances precision and recall (their harmonic mean).
false alarm: A ticket for something that did not really happen (a false positive).
missed: A real violation for which the system made no ticket (a false negative).
caught: A real violation that the system matched with a ticket of the same kind at about the same time.
benchmark: Running the whole system on clips whose true events are known, then counting caught, missed and false alarms.
LOAR: Logging and Organization Accuracy Rate: of the caught events, the share logged with the right violation, the right vehicle and the exact plate text.
CER: Character Error Rate: how many plate characters were read wrongly, as a share of all true characters.
WER: Word Error Rate: the share of plates that were not read exactly right (here a whole plate is one 'word').
ONNX: A standard file format (.onnx) that stores a trained model so many programs can run it without the training software.
ONNX Runtime: The program that runs .onnx models quickly on a CPU or a graphics card.
PyTorch: The deep-learning library that Ultralytics, DeepSORT and EasyOCR are built on. Used for training.
GPU: The graphics chip. It does the heavy math of models far faster than the normal processor (CPU).
CUDA: NVIDIA's technology that lets programs use its graphics cards for general math.
VRAM: The memory of the graphics card.
AMP: Automatic mixed precision: training with smaller numbers where safe, which is faster and uses less memory.
specialist model: A small model with one job, run only on the cropped part of the picture it needs (helmet, plate or cabin).
cascade: Steps in a line: one general detector first, then specialist models only on the crops that need them.
registry: The part of the backend that loads the right model files when the system starts.
manifest: A small list file that says which model file is active, or which datasets to download and how to map them.
tracking: Following the same object from frame to frame and giving it one steady ID number.
track ID: The steady number the tracker gives one vehicle for as long as it stays on screen.
DeepSORT: A tracker that matches objects between frames using where they should be (motion) and what they look like (a fingerprint).
ByteTrack: A tracker that matches objects between frames only by how much their boxes overlap. Fast, but it ignores looks.
ReID: Re-identification: deciding whether two pictures show the same car.
fingerprint: A short list of numbers a network computes from a picture. Pictures of the same car should give close numbers.
Market-1501: A public dataset of pedestrians. The original DeepSORT look-network was trained on pictures like these.
supervision: A Python library of computer-vision helpers. We use its ByteTrack and its polygon-zone test.
OCR: Optical Character Recognition: reading the letters and digits in a picture.
EasyOCR: A free OCR library. We use it to read the characters of a cropped licence plate.
super-resolution: Using a model to make a small, blurry picture bigger and sharper.
GAN: Generative Adversarial Network: two networks compete, one draws images and one judges them, until the drawn images look real.
Real-ESRGAN: A GAN-based super-resolution model that upscales pictures 4 times.
LapSRN: A super-resolution network that enlarges a picture step by step. We use its 8-times version.
Lanczos: A classic, non-AI way to enlarge a picture smoothly.
heuristic: A rule of thumb with numbers somebody chose and measured. It gives a good-enough answer without a learned model.
zone: A shape (polygon) the operator draws on the camera picture to say where a rule applies. Also called ROI, region of interest.
polygon: A shape made of straight sides, stored as a list of its corner points.
ledger: Our notebook for one vehicle: its positions over time, its votes, its class and what it is suspected of.
ground point: The bottom-centre of a vehicle's box, where its tyres touch the road. All zone tests use this point.
vote: Deciding from many looks instead of one: for example 'bad in at least 60% of the last 10 looks'.
pending: A suspicion that is not final yet. It becomes a ticket only if it still holds when the vehicle leaves the picture.
safety gate: A rule that skips a check when the picture cannot support it, for example a tinted windshield that hides the driver.
heading: The direction a vehicle is travelling, as an arrow (a unit vector) computed from its recent path.
dot product: A number that tells whether two arrows point the same way (positive), at right angles (zero) or opposite ways (negative).
px/s: Pixels per second: how fast a box moves across the picture.
grid cell: One small square of the picture when it is cut into a regular grid.
co-motion: Moving together: a person who travels in the same direction and at a similar speed as a vehicle.
HSV: A way to describe colour as hue (which colour), saturation (how strong) and value (how bright). Good for finding red, amber or green.
Hz: Times per second. A light that blinks at 1 Hz switches on and off once every second.
evidence frame: A saved photo of a flagged vehicle, with its zones and the 'why' boxes drawn on it.
ticket: The record the system creates for one vehicle: its violations, plate text and evidence frames. A human reviews it.
forensic analysis: Running a recorded video through the whole pipeline from start to end, with every frame processed.
wizard: The step-by-step screen in the dashboard where you pick violations, draw zones and start an analysis.
harvest: Our tool that collects pictures from finished analyses so a person can check them and add them to a dataset.
human-in-the-loop: A design where a person checks the system's work before anything final happens.
FastAPI: The Python web framework our backend server is built with.
SQLite: A small database stored in a single file.
Flutter: Google's toolkit for building apps. Our dashboard, citizen app and visualizer use it.
RTSP: Real Time Streaming Protocol: the way IP cameras and CCTV recorders send live video over a network.
CCTV: Closed-circuit television: fixed security or traffic cameras.
FFmpeg: A free tool that converts and compresses video.
frame: One still picture of a video. A video is many frames shown quickly, about 25 every second.
stream: Video that is sent while it is being filmed, instead of a finished file.
IP address: The number that tells a network where a device is, like 192.168.1.20. A network camera has one.
port: A numbered door on a device. One address can offer several services, each on its own door, for example 554 for camera video.
lag: The delay between something happening on the road and showing on screen.
MediaMTX: A small free program that receives a video stream from one place and hands it to others. We use it as the relay between our AI and the dashboard.
ONVIF: An industry standard that lets cameras and software from different makers work together.
DVR: Digital video recorder: the box that stores CCTV footage and can also pass the live pictures on. An NVR is the same for network cameras.
MJPEG: A way to send video as a stream of ordinary JPEG pictures. Simple and widely supported, but it uses a lot of bandwidth.
H.264: The most common way to compress video so it can travel over a network.
VS Code: The code editor many developers use. The 'Open in VS Code' links jump straight to the line.
Roboflow: A website where the community shares labelled datasets. Many of ours come from its Universe section.
Mendeley Data: A research-data host run by Elsevier. Datasets there have a DOI and a citation.
Zenodo: A research-data host run by CERN. Datasets there have a DOI and a citation.
Open Images: Google's large public photo collection with labelled boxes, including licence plates.
CC BY 4.0: Creative Commons licence: you may use and change the work freely if you credit the author.
MIT licence: A very permissive software licence: use freely, keep the copyright notice.
trust grade: Our own rating of a data source: A = peer-reviewed or official host, B = community upload with an open licence and a named author, C = unclear origin.
RA 4136: Republic Act 4136, the Land Transportation and Traffic Code of 1964. The base law for most of our violations.
LTO: Land Transportation Office, the national agency for vehicles and licences.
MMDA: Metropolitan Manila Development Authority. Its traffic rules apply in Metro Manila.
JAO 2014-01: Joint Administrative Order 2014-01: the uniform list of traffic violation names and fines used on tickets.
LGU: Local Government Unit: a city or municipality, such as Zamboanga City.
NCAP: No Contact Apprehension Policy: giving tickets from camera evidence without stopping the driver.
RA 10173: The Data Privacy Act of 2012. It governs how personal data, such as plate numbers and photos, may be collected and shown.
